endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Focus AI policy dissemination on making the governance process easy and visible; create a simple, low-friction intake pathway so staff want to use the official process.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Update GAI acceptable use policies to address proprietary and open-source GAI technologies and data, and contractors, consultants, and other third-party personnel.

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: a) U se of automated decision-making systems that determine coverage limits, make claim determinations, and engage in benefit design should be publicly reported, based on easily accessible evidence-based clinical guidelines (as opposed to proprietary payor criteria), and disclosed to both patients and their physician in a way that is easy to understand.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing the EU AI Act in a comprehensive cancer center through an institutional governance framework
endorsements.quote: Define approved use cases, prohibited uses, data-entry restrictions, validation requirements, and traceability rules for LLM-based tools.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations and Fundamental Principles of Large Language Models in Medical Education: Viewpoint
endorsements.quote: Establish policies and guidelines: educational institutions should establish specific LLM usage policies and guidelines based on a unified set of ethical principles to specify the legal and ethical use of LLMs as well as to prohibit any form of academic misconduct clearly and explain the corresponding consequences.

endorsements.title: Harm Reduction Strategies for Thoughtful Use of Large Language Models in the Medical Domain: Perspectives for Patients and Clinicians
endorsements.quote: Establishing clear institutional use cases and risk-stratified guidelines: health care organizations must develop, disseminate, and enforce clear policies defining approved LLM tools, permitted use cases (eg, drafting noncritical notes and literature search) versus high-risk or prohibited uses (eg, autonomous diagnosis or treatment planning), and required safeguards for each [ 54 ].

endorsements.title: AI-Assisted Formative Assessment in Clinical Education: From Algorithms to Agency
endorsements.quote: Institutions should specify which AI tools are approved, what data may be entered, who can access learner outputs, and how long learner data are retained.

endorsements.title: The VIBE-HI framework: a conceptual model for evaluating vibe coding appropriateness, quality, and safety in health informatics
endorsements.quote: In parallel, three actions are available now: health systems should adopt tiered acceptable-use policies that name a tier, a role, and an owner; regulators should clarify how generative, non-deterministic clinical tools enter existing frameworks before the EU AI Act’s August 2027 deadline; and professional bodies should incorporate agentic-coding competencies into clinical-informatics training, building on recent competency work ( Cao et al., 2026 ).

endorsements.title: Generative AI in psychiatric education: balancing risks and benefits for responsible integration
endorsements.quote: Policy and governance Develop clear institutional usage policies; establish an AI ethics oversight committee Ensure consistent, responsible use; address gaps in accountability

endorsements.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence Integration in Medical Student Education in Somalia and Low-Resource Settings: A Context-Sensitive Implementation Framework
endorsements.issuer: Advances in medical education and practice
endorsements.quote: The group should maintain an approved-use matrix that distinguishes low-risk uses such as formative explanation from restricted uses such as assessment generation and prohibited uses such as entering identifiable patient data into unapproved public systems.

evidence.title: Cognitive Stitching: Informal AI Integration in Everyday Clinical Reasoning
evidence.outcome: Clinicians' use of unsanctioned personal-device and consumer AI tools in diagnostic reasoning
evidence.effect: AI frequently enters clinical practice through informal use of personal mobile devices and consumer applications rather than officially deployed hospital systems, when institutional platforms give insufficient interpretive support.
evidence.quote: The analysis shows that AI frequently enters clinical practice not through officially deployed hospital systems but through informal practices involving personal mobile devices and widely accessible consumer applications.

evidence.title: Use of large language models by academic hospitalists: results of a multicenter survey
evidence.outcome: Hospitalist LLM use in practice and barriers including policy uncertainty and lack of secure tools
evidence.effect: 67.1% (170 respondents) ever used an LLM clinically; 48.6% cited uncertainty around institutional policies and 43.1% lack of access to secure applications as barriers.
evidence.quote: Lack of trust in outputs (49.8%), uncertainty around institutional policies (48.6%), and lack of access to secure applications (43.1%) were cited as the most frequent barriers to using LLMs in practice.

evidence.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Use of Artificial Intelligence Among Adult and Pediatric Hematologists in Türkiye: A National Cross- Sectional Survey
evidence.outcome: Entry of patient data into non-approved public chatbots
evidence.effect: 48.6% had entered patient data into non-approved public chatbots (8.2% identifiable).
evidence.quote: Nearly half (48.6%) had entered patient data into non-approved public chatbots (8.2% identifiable), whereas only 4.8% reported a written institutional AI policy.

evidence.title: A survey of Large Language Model use in a hospital, research, and teaching campus
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of LLM use in work contexts among campus staff and students, ahead of governance
evidence.effect: Over 90% of respondents had heard of LLM tools and about two-thirds had used them in their work on campus; guidelines and governance are needed to keep up with practice.
evidence.quote: Our findings show LLM tools are already widely used on our campus.

evidence.title: The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Plastic Surgery Education: Insights From Program Directors and Residents
evidence.outcome: Presence of formal AI policies versus resident independent AI use
evidence.effect: 88% of PDs reported no formal AI policy; 50% of residents used AI independently, mostly ChatGPT (50%), without institutional guidance.
evidence.quote: Only 8% of PDs reported screening residency applications for AI-generated content, and 88% indicated their programs had no formal policies on AI use.

evidence.title: Use, knowledge and perception of large language models in clinical practice: a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey among clinicians in Switzerland
evidence.outcome: Availability of workplace LLM guidelines reported by clinicians amid frequent LLM use
evidence.effect: 225 (32.8%) reported frequent LLM use, while only 42 (6%) reported availability of workplace LLM guidelines.
evidence.quote: Among 685 participants (response rate 29.0%), 225 (32.8%) reported frequent use of LLMs, 25 (3.6%) reported having used a specific medical LLM and 42 (6%) reported the availability of workplace LLM guidelines.

evidence.title: Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence in Medical Documentation: A Cross-Sectional Study of Healthcare Professionals
evidence.outcome: Current clinician use of AI for clinical or administrative work without official approval
evidence.effect: 52% (n = 33) had used AI for clinical or administrative work; 70% (n = 44) would use it if officially approved; institutional guidance reported by only 11%.
evidence.quote: While only 52% (n = 33) had used AI for clinical or administrative work, 70% (n = 44) indicated they would do so if officially approved.

evidence.title: Patterns of AI Use in Clinical Work by Hospitalists: Survey Study
evidence.outcome: Proportion of hospitalists using unsanctioned AI tools in clinical practice without institutional endorsement
evidence.effect: 36 of 54 respondents (66.7%; 95% CI 53.4%-77.8%) reported using AI in clinical practice; OpenEvidence used by 28/54 (51.9%), ChatGPT by 4/54 (7.4%), without institutional oversight.
evidence.quote: Two-thirds of hospitalists organically adopted AI despite the absence of institutional oversight.

evidence.title: Large Language Model Use and Training Needs Among Rheumatologists: An APLAR Young Rheumatologists International Survey
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of LLM use and presence of institutional LLM policies among rheumatologists
evidence.effect: 89.6% reported prior LLM use, while only 9.9% reported established institutional policies on LLM use.
evidence.quote: While usage is widespread, only 9.9% reported established institutional policies on LLMs use.

evidence.title: Health Professional Students' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence During Clinical Placements: Cross-Sectional Online Survey Study
evidence.outcome: Unsanctioned generative AI use by students during clinical placements
evidence.effect: 204 (52.6%) of 388 students reported using GenAI during clinical placements; 23.5% of users reported disclosing patient-identifying information.
evidence.quote: Overall, 204 (52.6%) students reported using GenAI during clinical placements.

evidence.title: Conversational artificial intelligence in the operating room: an exploratory cross-sectional single-center survey among anesthesiology residents
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of conversational AI use in the OR with limited institutional policies
evidence.effect: Operating room use was reported by 58.1% (95% CI 47.6-68.0%) of 86 residents; institutional policies appeared limited.
evidence.quote: Conversational AI use in the operating room was reported by 58.1% (95% CI 47.6-68.0%).

evidence.title: Shadow AI in Swedish Health Care: Qualitative Analysis of Physicians' Free-Text Answers
evidence.outcome: Physicians' use of unauthorized AI tools (Shadow AI) for clinical and administrative purposes
evidence.effect: Physicians reported using unauthorized AI for clinical decision support (differential diagnoses, rare cases), patient communication, documentation, research and curiosity; use compensated for perceived gaps in institutional systems.
evidence.quote: Physicians use Shadow AI for several purposes, which we grouped into 4 categories: clinical work and decision-making, administrative work, research and professional development, and technological interest and curiosity.

evidence.title: Adoption, use, and barriers to artificial intelligence and telemedicine in Italian primary care: a cross-sectional national survey
evidence.outcome: Spontaneous, unsanctioned ChatGPT adoption by primary care physicians relative to institutional governance
evidence.effect: 51.2% of respondents spontaneously adopted ChatGPT, mainly for administrative burden; younger age and scientific engagement predicted adoption; adoption outpaces institutional governance.
evidence.quote: These findings suggest that the spontaneous adoption of generative AI currently outpaces institutional governance, highlighting the need for targeted training and GDPR-compliant infrastructures within the DM77/2022 reform framework.

evidence.title: General-Purpose Artificial Intelligence Use in Routine Mental Health Practice Among Australian Clinicians: Mixed Methods Study
evidence.outcome: Clinician use of general-purpose AI amid workplace governance and privacy concerns
evidence.effect: 43.5% (121/278) reported daily administrative/clinician-support AI use and 33.1% (92/278) daily client-facing use; interviewees reported privacy, data security concerns and uneven workplace governance.
evidence.quote: Participants also raised concerns about privacy, data security, accuracy, client acceptability, overreliance, loss of human judgment, and uneven workplace governance.
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents (mental health professionals); plus 12 interviewed clinicians

evidence.title: Generative artificial intelligence in medicine: a mixed-methods survey of UK general practitioners
evidence.outcome: GP use of unsanctioned non-medical-grade AI for clinical tasks
evidence.effect: One-fifth of GPs reported having used AI for clinical practice; a portion used non-medical grade technology for clinical tasks.
evidence.quote: Many GPs reported a lack of knowledge and experience with this technology, although a portion already used non-medical grade technology for clinical tasks, with the risks that this entails.

evidence.title: AI adoption among French oncology pharmacists: A national survey
evidence.venue: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
evidence.outcome: Prevalence of shadow AI use and access to validated tools among oncology pharmacists
evidence.effect: 65.3% operated within a shadow AI framework; only 17.3% had access to fit-for-purpose validated tools; AI adoption 94.7%.
evidence.quote: However, 65.3% operated within a shadow AI framework, while only 17.3% had access to fit-for-purpose validated tools.

evidence.title: Informal use of generative artificial intelligence by nursing interns during clinical placement: A multi-stakeholder interpretive description
evidence.outcome: Informal, unsanctioned generative AI use by nursing interns on personal devices amid lack of governance
evidence.effect: Interns used generative AI on personal devices during clinical placement while institutional governance had not kept pace; participants across all stakeholder groups called for tiered governance.
evidence.quote: Interns use it on personal devices, yet institutional governance has not kept pace.
evidence.sample_unit: interview participants (nursing interns, preceptors, head nurses, administrators, IT specialists, quality officer)

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether publishing an acceptable-use policy and approved tools list reduces unsanctioned AI use or exposure of patient information. Seventeen surveys and interview studies show that clinicians and trainees commonly use unapproved AI tools and sometimes enter patient data, often where no policy exists.

perspectives.view: All 17 studies are level 3 surveys or qualitative studies that document shadow AI use, and none compares settings with and without a published policy. Nine endorsements, mostly commentaries, support the practice. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about the effect of the practice cannot be rated because no study tests it.

In a survey of 146 hematologists, 48.6% had entered patient data into non-approved public chatbots, and 8.2% had entered identifiable data. Among 388 French students, 23.5% of GenAI users reported disclosing patient-identifying information. These figures show that the exposure exists, but no study shows that a written policy stops data before it leaves the organization.

Among US hospitalists, 48.6% cited uncertainty about institutional policy and 43.1% cited lack of secure applications as barriers. Swedish and Chinese clinicians described unsanctioned tools filling gaps in institutional systems. These findings suggest a policy may work only when paired with approved tools and a low-burden intake route, as the CHAI playbook advises.

Among 63 UK health professionals, 70% said they would use AI if officially approved, and 11% reported institutional guidance. Among French oncology pharmacists, 65.3% worked within shadow AI and 17.3% had access to validated tools. These data suggest that most of the cost may lie in supplying vetted tools rather than in drafting the policy.

NIST AI 600-1 advises updating generative AI acceptable-use policies to cover proprietary and open-source tools and third-party personnel. The CHAI playbooks rate policy dissemination as a must. Reported coverage is low, with 6% of 685 Swiss clinicians and 9.9% of 767 Asia-Pacific rheumatologists reporting workplace guidelines or policies.

The reported rates at which clinicians and students enter patient information into public chatbots point to a privacy risk that patients have no direct way to detect. A published approved tools list would give patients a basis to ask which tools handle their records. No study has measured whether publication changes patient trust or data exposure.

None of the 17 hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A framework for Somalia and low-resource settings recommends an approved-use matrix, but it is a commentary and not a test. Whether policies reach staff in under-resourced settings has not been examined.

commentary.research_gap: Controlled or stepped-wedge studies across several health systems are needed to compare unapproved AI use and PHI exposure before and after publication of an acceptable-use policy and approved tools list. Outcomes could include audited data-loss events, self-reported unapproved use, and uptake of approved tools. Such studies should separate the effect of the written policy from the effect of providing secure alternatives.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies also do not report on these groups. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether a published policy reduces shadow AI use among their staff or protects their patients' data.
